canonical.name: Measurability of the centered maximal function is a theorem, and the continuity of ball averages is scaffolded separately so that the openness proof is not hidden inside a definition.
The page keeps the centered and uncentered maximal functions distinct but explicitly comparable, so later pages may cite whichever convention they need without silent identification.
The weak $(1,1)$ inequality is scaffolded with the design's safe $5^n$ constant and no optimality claim, even though some sources prove sharper numerical constants.
Failure of strong type $(1,1)$ stays on the A page as a general counterexample, not only as the unit-interval witness on the examples page.

Marcinkiewicz and Riesz-Thorin are separate items: the former is the real-variable weak-to-strong interpolation theorem for sublinear operators, while the latter is the exact linear strip-interpolation theorem with its own self-contained three-lines argument.
The differentiation theorem is scaffolded in the three-step form named by the design: continuous compactly supported functions, MT-15 density, and maximal-inequality control of the error set.
The Lebesgue-point theorem is stated at the class level and its proof is forced to produce one null set for the whole theorem by taking a countable union over rational constants.
Density points, nicely shrinking families, differentiation of measures, and the $L^1$ first FTC all remain on the A page rather than being pushed to MT-18 or MT-19.

The B page keeps the design's explicit maximal-function, spike, class-level rationals, endpoint-density, compact positive-measure sharpness, Steinhaus, density-half, and null-set divergence leaves. The fat-Cantor boundary-density computation is not scaffolded separately here because the current closure does not make that computation cheap or source-backed.
